# Martin Ferret

> Martin Ferret is a French TypeScript expert focused on type-checking performance, a contributor to Microsoft's TypeScript DOM types, and Lead Content Owner for the JavaScript and TypeScript certifications at Certificates.dev.

Contact: mferret.pro@gmail.com. Last updated 2026-11-11. Full text of the key pages: https://martinferret.github.io/llms-full.txt

## Services
- TypeScript performance audit: measure type-checking time and memory on the team's real codebase, find the types and files that cost the most, deliver a prioritized fix list.
- TypeScript 7 migration: measure TypeScript 6 vs 7 on the team's project, check memory in CI, plan a safe migration.
- Type-checking budget in CI: budgets based on the compiler's counters, with a tolerance calibrated on the project, so a pull request can't silently slow the build down.
- Team training and workshops: advanced TypeScript and type performance, for Angular, React and Node.js teams.

## How a project starts
We start with a short call about your codebase and what slows it down. The method is the same one behind the public experiments: measure, isolate one cause, fix it without weakening types, and publish the numbers to your team. See the merged fixes on Work, the experiments in the Lab, and the talks I give on Invite me to speak.

## Short bio
I'm a TypeScript developer focused on type-checking performance and TypeScript 7. I measure what makes TypeScript slow, then fix it: I run a public TypeScript Performance Lab with reproducible experiments, and my fixes to TypeScript's DOM types have been merged into Microsoft's TypeScript-DOM-lib-generator. I'm Lead Content Owner for the JavaScript and TypeScript certifications at Certificates.dev, and I've spent seven years building large-scale enterprise applications with TypeScript, Angular and Spring Boot. I also host What's up TypeScript France, an online TypeScript meetup.

## Talks you can book
Each one can run as a talk, online or on site, in English or French. Every talk is built on the Lab's published experiments; past appearances are on Speaking.

## The DOM Is Lying to Your Types
Level
Expert
Format
30 to 45 min
Every TypeScript project trusts lib.dom.d.ts, but it isn't written by hand: a generator turns web specifications into types, and that translation is where bugs hide. Optional parameters that throw, iterables typed as arrays, return types lost on the way. I fix these bugs upstream in Microsoft's generator. In this talk, I show how WebIDL becomes TypeScript, why the spec and not MDN is the source of truth, how to prove a DOM type is wrong, and how a fix travels from a pull request to your editor.

## Your Types Have a Performance Budget. You're Just Not Measuring It.
Level
Expert
Format
30 to 45 min, also as a half-day workshop
A one-line type change can multiply type-checking cost by ten without breaking a test: real projects shipped 23 times more instantiations and CI jobs that crashed. We budget bundle size and page speed, so why not types? TypeScript 6's counters are deterministic: same code, same numbers on any machine. With TypeScript 7, I measured small variations on large test suites, and I'm investigating how much tolerance a CI budget needs. I show how to measure the cost of your types, find the generic that dominates it, and fail a pull request before your build slows down.

## Your AI Agent Is Slowing Down Your Compiler
Level
Intermediate to expert
Format
30 to 45 min
Typed AI agents are everywhere: tools described with schemas, structured outputs inferred into TypeScript types, SDKs built on deeply generic APIs. Great for safety, but they can quietly crush your type-checker. I'm measuring what schemas, tool definitions and AI SDK types cost the TypeScript compiler as an agent grows from 1 to 50 tools, and which ways of writing them stay fast. You'll see the numbers, why some patterns explode, and how to keep agents fully typed and fast to build.

# TypeScript Performance Lab

URL: https://martinferret.github.io/lab/

## TypeScript Performance Lab
Each experiment ships its code, the exact command that produced the numbers, and the raw results with the machine they ran on.
See the experimentsHow it’s measured2 experimentsData generated Nov 11, 2026
Lab #001Confirmed−57%check time with TypeScript 7 after the fix
Lab #002Open question3.5×faster check of type-fest sources, TypeScript 7 vs 6
Lab #001Confirmed

## Typed events
−57%check time with TypeScript 7 after the fix
Yes. On an Apple M3 Pro (12 cores), inferring the event name from the generic parameter cut check time by 52% with TypeScript 6 and by 57% with TypeScript 7 (51% to 65% from the fastest and slowest runs); on a 1-core Intel Xeon, by 41% and 65%. The safety check passed on both machines, so the type safety is the same. Narrowing include to src also stopped TypeScript from reading a generated file the app never imports.
Read the experiment −52%890 ms430 msTypeScript 6−57%330 ms143 msTypeScript 7Before the fixAfter the fixMedian check time, lower is fasterOpened October 2026. Latest run: Apple M3 Pro, 12 cores, 36 GB, Node.js 22.23.3, Nov 9, 2026. 2 machines in total.
Lab #002Open question

## TypeScript 6 vs 7 on type-fest
3.5×faster check of type-fest sources, TypeScript 7 vs 6
Being re-measured The verdict below stays as published until the new results are in.
On an Apple M3 Pro (12 cores), TypeScript 7.0.2 checked the type-fest sources 3.5× faster than TypeScript 6.0.3 (0.484 s vs 1.67 s): 2.6× comes from the native compiler alone (single-threaded) and 1.3× from parallel checking. On the full suite with type tests, TypeScript 6 stops at Node.js's default heap limit (4.0 GiB); with a 16 GiB heap it finishes in 74.6 s, against 14.1 s for TypeScript 7 (5.3× faster), but TypeScript 7 peaks higher in memory (11.6 GiB RSS vs 10.4 GiB). Stays open until a second machine is measured with the same protocol.
Read the experiment 4.1× faster6.68 s1.61 sIntel Xeon3.5× faster1.67 s484 msApple M3 ProTypeScript 6TypeScript 7Median check time, lower is fasterLatest run: Apple M3 Pro, 12 cores, 36 GB, Node.js 22.23.3, Nov 11, 2026. 2 machines in total.
Method

## Same protocol, every experiment
Six rules that make a number worth publishing. The notebook's method page has the full protocol, and the lab repository has the scripts. To apply it to your own codebase, see Work with me.
Rule 1

## Pin everything
Compiler versions, external commits and machine context are recorded with every result.

Rule 2

## Measure the same way
Several runs of tsc with extended diagnostics per condition, after a discarded warm-up, conditions interleaved. Median reported with the range.

Rule 3

## Change one thing
A fix changes a single thing and keeps the same type safety.

Rule 4

## Prove type safety
A safety file lists usages that must still fail to compile. The run stops if one passes.

Rule 5

## Publish any verdict
Confirmed, rejected or open. Negative results are published too.

Rule 6

## Know the limits
Compare conditions on the same machine only. Counters may differ across compilers.

# About

URL: https://martinferret.github.io/about/

## About Martin Ferret
Martin Ferret is a French TypeScript expert focused on type-checking performance, a contributor to Microsoft's TypeScript DOM types, and Lead Content Owner for the JavaScript and TypeScript certifications at Certificates.dev.
Work with me Invite me to speakMartin Ferret France, working remotely across EuropeHe works on how fast TypeScript checks types. He builds small experiments that isolate one cause of slowness, measures it on TypeScript 6 and 7, and publishes the result with the raw numbers in the TypeScript Performance Lab, including when the hypothesis turns out to be wrong.
When the cause sits in TypeScript’s own type definitions, he fixes it there: his pull requests to the DOM type definitions are merged into Microsoft’s TypeScript-DOM-lib-generator, listed on Work. He has spent seven years building large-scale enterprise applications with TypeScript and Angular.
He is the author of 30 articles on the Certificates.dev blog, listed on Writing. He co-hosted Devpreneur, a French-language podcast about entrepreneurship for developers, with Alain Chautard. He runs What's up TypeScript France, a free online meetup in French.
Open sourceContributor to TypeScript’s DOM types

Method

## How I work
The same loop for every slowdown, from the first measurement to the published result.
Step 1

## Measure
Run tsc with extended diagnostics on a real project and record check time, memory and instantiations.

Step 2

## Isolate
Shrink the slowdown to one cause in a small experiment, with a safety file proving the types stay as strict.

Step 3

## Fix upstream
When the cause lives in TypeScript’s own types, open a pull request there, not a workaround.

Step 4

## Publish
Ship the raw numbers and the machine they ran on, whatever the verdict.

TimelineEvery contribution, talk and experiment, by dateEach entry links to its source.Open the timeline Contact: mferret.pro@gmail.com. For a talk, a workshop or a podcast, see Invite me.
